question: Why do nurses use transmission-based precautions?

options.A: To stop the spread of specific targeted pathogens
options.B: To replace standard handwashing routines entirely
options.C: To isolate healthy staff members from routine work
options.D: To reduce hospital utility and cleaning costs

explanation: You've got this! These extra precautions are added on top of standard care whenever we are dealing with known or suspected germs that need special containment. Great job!

question: When is the right time to start transmission-based precautions for a patient?

options.A: At the first sign of symptoms or upon suspicion of infection
options.B: After public health officers visit the ward
options.C: When the patient requests a private hospital room
options.D: Only after laboratory confirmation is fully finalized

explanation: Spot on! Waiting for lab results takes time, and germs don't wait. As soon as you suspect an infection, start precautions right away to keep everyone safe.

question: Which patients should receive standard precautions in the hospital?

options.A: Patients admitted to surgical wards only
options.B: Only patients with confirmed viral infections
options.C: Every patient in the healthcare facility

explanation: Exactly! Standard precautions are universal. Treat every patient as if their body fluids could carry infection, keeping both them and yourself protected.

question: Why is hand hygiene considered the most important part of standard precautions?

options.A: It completely sterilizes the skin of the hands
options.B: It removes transient microorganisms picked up from surfaces
options.C: It eliminates the need for wearing medical gloves
options.D: It neutralizes airborne toxins before inhalation

explanation: Well done! Washing or sanitizing your hands physically washes away the hitchhiking germs you pick up from touching patients and equipment, stopping cross-contamination in its tracks.

question: What kind of germs usually require contact precautions on the ward?
explanation: You got it! Germs that laugh at common antibiotics love to hitch a ride on hands and hospital equipment, so we use strict contact precautions to keep them from spreading.

question: You are caring for a wound infection patient on contact precautions. What should you do before stepping out of their room?

options.A: Wash the patient's wound with sterile saline solution
options.B: Leave the isolation gown on to wear for the next patient
options.C: Remove gloves and gown inside the room and perform hand hygiene
options.D: Spray the hallway floor with a strong chlorine disinfectant

explanation: Spot on! Always take off your protective gear before you cross that doorway so you don't carry any unwanted souvenir germs out into the hallway.

question: How far do infectious respiratory droplets typically travel through the air?
explanation: That's right! Respiratory droplets are quite heavy, so gravity pulls them down fast. They rarely travel farther than a meter from the person coughing or talking.

question: What mask must you wear when entering a room under droplet precautions?

options.B: A full body hazardous materials suit
options.D: A standard surgical or medical mask

explanation: Correct! A simple surgical mask does a great job blocking those heavy respiratory droplets from landing in your nose and mouth.

question: Which disease requires you to use airborne precautions?
explanation: Well done! TB is caused by tiny airborne bugs that hang suspended in the air for a long time, meaning we need special room ventilation and respirators to stay safe.

question: How does a negative pressure isolation room stop airborne diseases from escaping?

options.A: It draws air into the room and stops it from escaping into the hallway
options.B: It raises the room temperature to kill suspended viral particles
options.C: It pushes clean air outward into the public hospital corridors
options.D: It creates a vacuum that destroys bacteria before they multiply

explanation: You nailed it! Think of it like a gentle draft pulling inward; when the door opens, air rushes inside rather than letting contaminated room air leak out into the hall.

question: When taking off your personal protective equipment (doffing), which item should come off FIRST?
explanation: Spot on! Your gloves are the dirtiest item since they touched the patient directly, so peeling them off first keeps the rest of your cleanup process safe.

question: What is the correct order for putting on (donning) your PPE before entering an isolation room?

options.A: Mask first, then gloves, gown, and eye protection
options.B: Gloves first, then gown, mask, and protective eyewear
options.C: Eye protection first, followed by gloves, gown, and mask
options.D: Gown first, then mask or respirator, eye protection, and gloves

explanation: Great job! You start by covering your body with the gown, secure your breathing and eyes, and pull your glove cuffs over the gown sleeves last so there are no skin gaps.

question: What should a patient with a respiratory infection wear when moving outside their isolation room?

options.A: Cover the patient completely with a sterile plastic sheet
options.B: Transport the patient only during night shift hours
options.C: Ensure the patient walks without any staff assistance
options.D: Have the patient wear a surgical mask during transport

explanation: Exactly! Having the patient wear a mask traps any stray respiratory droplets right at the source while you walk them through the hospital corridors.

question: Which hospital objects are considered high-touch surfaces that need frequent cleaning?
explanation: You got it! Bed rails, call buttons, and door handles are touched constantly by everyone, making them hot spots for passing germs along.

question: How can you keep hands clean in a clinic when the running water supply stops?

options.A: Use set-up handwashing stations like Veronica buckets and alcohol rubs
options.B: Wipe hands clean with ordinary office paper towels
options.C: Wear the same pair of examination gloves all day long
options.D: Skip handwashing until municipal water lines are fully restored

explanation: Brilliant! Improvised running-water setups like Veronica buckets and alcohol-based rubs keep patient care safe even when the taps go dry.

question: Why do community health clinics use safety boxes?

options.A: To keep surgical instruments sterile during rainy seasons
options.B: To separate paper trash from general food waste
options.C: To prevent needle-stick injuries and unsafe sharp disposal
options.D: To store expired medications safely away from children

explanation: Spot on! Puncture-proof safety boxes protect both healthcare workers and the local community from accidental needle sticks and blood infections.
